idiom_name: single-owner worker/task + #private implementation methods (visibility only, no lock)
implementation_notes: TypeScript erases at runtime, so the pattern's two halves land differently: the visibility half is strongly expressible (#private methods cannot be reached from outside the class, while private is compile-time only), but the lock half has no language support at all, because the underlying JavaScript runtime has no synchronously acquirable lock over shared mutable state. Ordinary Node and browser components are single-threaded and interleave only at await, so intra-component calls cannot deadlock on a component lock; async-lock libraries reintroduce the non-reentrant lock and its nested-acquisition deadlock, and shared memory requires SharedArrayBuffer plus Atomics, which is lock-free by construction. The useful adaptation is ownership: one task or worker owns the state, public methods enqueue commands, private methods run to completion inside the owner.
pitfalls: #private keeps outside callers out but not the class itself: a public method that awaits another public method still queues behind its own pending command and deadlocks the queue.
A promise-chain or async-mutex lock is not reentrant, so the nested-acquisition deadlock the pattern prevents on threads reappears unchanged.
SharedArrayBuffer needs cross-origin isolation (COOP/COEP) and Atomics.wait is unavailable on the main thread, so blocking coordination has no portable form there.
worker_threads do not share module state: each worker has its own instances, so 'one shared component' is a message-passing design rather than a mutable shared object.
alternative: Keep the state single-owner: a dedicated worker (or a serialized promise queue in one task) owns the component and callers exchange messages or commands with it; #private helpers then live inside the owner and no lock exists to re-acquire. If shared memory is genuinely required, use Atomics on a SharedArrayBuffer for lock-free coordination instead of a re-entrant lock.
